subject: electrical-computer
audience: FE Electrical and Computer candidates and engineering students
title: The Higher-Gain Loop That Crossed Into Instability
featured_title: THE HIGHER-GAIN LOOP THAT CROSSED INTO INSTABILITY

presentation.challenge: Increasing gain improved response—until the characteristic equation crossed the stability limit.

practice.primary_question: Why can increasing loop gain make a unity-feedback control system unstable?
practice.typical_exam_trap: Assuming that larger feedback gain always improves response without checking closed-loop pole stability.

case_dna.target_misconception: Increasing positive controller gain in a negative-feedback loop always improves response while preserving stability.
case_dna.why_plausible: Higher gain often reduces steady-state error, so it is easy to assume more gain is always beneficial.
case_dna.contradicting_evidence: For unity feedback with G(s)=K/[s(s+1)(s+3)], the characteristic polynomial is s^3+4s^2+3s+K. Routh-Hurwitz requires K>0 and 12-K>0, so 0<K<12.
case_dna.corrected_model: Controller gain must satisfy both performance and stability constraints. Form the closed-loop characteristic polynomial and test stability before increasing gain.

problem_statement: A unity negative-feedback plant has G(s)=K/[s(s+1)(s+3)]. A tuning note raises K to 20 to reduce tracking error. The closed loop then oscillates and diverges. Derive the characteristic equation, use the Routh criterion to find the stable gain range, and choose a gain that remains stable.

gates.label: Incident
gates.heading: More gain reduced error—then the loop became unstable.
gates.prompt: What must be checked before accepting the larger gain?

options.label: Form 1+G(s)=0 and apply the Routh-Hurwitz criterion
options.reason: Closed-loop stability depends on the roots of the characteristic polynomial.

options.label: A larger positive K always increases stability in negative feedback
options.reason: Negative feedback does not guarantee stability for arbitrary gain.

options.label: Only the numerator K determines stability
options.reason: Stability is determined by the closed-loop characteristic equation.

gates.label: Predict
gates.heading: Predict the stability threshold
gates.prompt: For s^3+4s^2+3s+K, what upper gain boundary K makes the Routh s^1 row go to zero?

gates.label: Experiment
gates.heading: Increase K through the boundary
gates.result: The Routh boundary occurs at K=12. Values above this boundary violate the stability condition.

gates.label: Gap
gates.heading: Derive the stable gain range
gates.prompt: For s^3+4s^2+3s+K, the Routh s^1 first-column term is (12-K)/4. Enter the upper stability boundary for K.
gates.success: The stable range is 0 < K < 12. K=20 is unstable.
gates.hint: Require every first-column Routh entry to be positive.

gates.label: Evidence
gates.heading: The Routh table exposes the gain limit

gates.label: Redline
gates.heading: Correct the tuning note
report: C1. The loop uses unity negative feedback.
C2. Increasing K can reduce steady-state error.
C3. Therefore K can be increased to 20 without a stability check.

claims.label: C2
claims.reason: Higher gain can reduce error in many systems.

claims.label: C3
claims.reason: Performance improvement does not remove the need to test closed-loop stability.

evidence_choices.label: Routh-Hurwitz gives the stable range 0<K<12
evidence_choices.reason: This directly limits the allowable gain.

correction.template: The gain must remain below {kmax} for this closed-loop characteristic polynomial to satisfy the Routh condition.

gates.label: Design Fix
gates.heading: Choose a stable positive gain
gates.constraint: Keep the same plant and unity-feedback architecture.

options.label: Use K=12
options.reason: K=12 is the marginal boundary, not strictly stable by the positive first-column test.

gates.label: Transfer
gates.heading: Apply the stability-range idea
gates.prompt: If a Routh test gives 0<K<8, which gain is strictly inside the stable range?
gates.explanation: A stable tuning point must satisfy the strict inequalities produced by the Routh test.

gates.label: Sign Off
gates.heading: Sign off the stability check
gates.confirmation: I confirm that controller gain must be checked against the closed-loop characteristic equation and stability criterion before tuning is accepted.

items.label: What failed
items.value: K=20 exceeded the closed-loop stability range.

items.label: What was assumed
items.value: More negative-feedback gain was assumed to be automatically safer.

items.label: Corrected model
items.value: Form the characteristic equation and verify stability before accepting gain changes.

seo.seo_title: Routh Stability Gain Limit: Why More Gain Became Unstable | FE E-034
seo.meta_description: Solve FE Case E-034: a unity-feedback loop becomes unstable at high gain. Use the Routh criterion to show the stable range is 0<K<12.
seo.focus_keyphrase: Routh stability gain limit FE exam
seo.excerpt: Higher controller gain can reduce error and still destabilize a feedback loop. The characteristic equation sets the allowable range.
seo.direct_answer: For unity feedback with G(s)=K/[s(s+1)(s+3)], the characteristic polynomial is s^3+4s^2+3s+K. Routh-Hurwitz requires K>0 and (12-K)/4>0, so the strictly stable range is 0<K<12.

faqs.q: What is the stable gain range for s^3+4s^2+3s+K?
Does negative feedback guarantee stability for any positive gain?
faqs.a: No. Stability must still be checked from the closed-loop characteristic equation.
